title: Pippin and the Harvest Cheese
markdown:
Lily’s house held a milky quiet. Her breath went like a small forest. Two pairs of eyes, which had been pretending to sleep, stopped pretending.

“Psst, Moss,” Pippin whispered. Whiskers twitched like fireflies with a plan. He was a rat of keen taste; tonight his dreams had been cheddar and secrets.

Moss, a squirrel whose tail conducted his thoughts, was already at the window. “I heard you. The moon is a sliver. The air smells of going. Lily sleeps. Now.”

They wriggled the gap. Dew. Night thrumming. Lamplight at the wood’s edge, past churchyard stones.

A line of mice shuffled, each with a minuscule candle, a procession for nothing Pippin could name. Diligence, unnecessarily dressed.

“What are they queuing for? There must be a shortcut.”

A portly mouse, spectacles askew, puffed. “Established protocols. Patience is a virtue. A well-ordered queue is its own reward.”

Moss nudged. “Too slow. Grander discoveries.” They wove around. The mice did not mind, which was, in its way, the protocol.

Deeper, lamps gave up and the moon took over, a pearl on velvet. Dapples. Then: cheerful murmur, tiny lanterns, a mandolin that had decided to be sweet.

Bunting on the branches, colourful as if the trees had been invited. In a clearing, voles, shrews, a gentle-eyed badger sat in a circle. On a mossy pedestal: a wheel of cheese, sun-kissed, a symphony pretending to be dairy.

Pippin’s eyes did a private festival. Dream-cheese, real. The creatures were watching a shy dormouse prepare to speak. The wheel looked, to a keen nose, quite alone.

“Unguarded. A prize, perhaps.”

Moss had a caution forming. Pippin did not wait for it. He darted, nudged, inhaled. The wheel wobbled, tipped, thudded into ferns.

“Oh, crumbs.” He began, without a second thought, to be sublime.

A hush. The badger ambled, kindly surprise on him like a coat. “Good heavens. Someone has absconded with the Harvest Festival Cheese.”

Pippin froze, gold on his nose. Moss’s tail drooped. “We thought it abandoned.”

The badger’s eyes knew something. He looked at rat, then nibble, and a chuckle moved like pebbles in a stream. “Abandoned? It was awaiting unveiling. A kind soul treated exposure as an oversight.”

He scooped what remained. Pippin kept a triumphant morsel, because of course. “Traditionally,” the badger said, twinkle admitted, “it is luck to taste first. You have brought fortune. Accidentally. Which is still fortune.”

Shock melted into amusement. The dormouse giggled. The candle-mice arrived, bewildered, at the end of their excellent queue.

They were not scolded. They were handed around the magnificent remainder until the community had a commencement after all. Pippin learned, without a speech, that the night’s best flavour was not only daring. It was also the warmth of being laughed with. He and Moss sat side by side, tummies considering a rest, bunting still at it, as if the cheese had been waiting and had not, in the end, minded being found too soon.
characters: Pippin (pet rat of keen taste), Moss (a squirrel whose tail conducts his thoughts)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
